attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The normalised version keeps all three parts: occasional leakage, the leakage still unresolved, and hallucinations still a problem. It is stated as present fact, not hedged.

contract.note: Reading 'private data' to include memorized personal data, and 'unresolved' as the underlying vulnerability remaining, is an ordinary plain reading. The contract openly flags the narrower meaning, confidential user conversations.

evidence.note: Extraction paper, available Nov 28, 2023, reports verified PII of dozens of individuals. The experiments predate the period, so this is background.
Researchers' dated assessment, inside the period: memorization and divergence remain vulnerabilities even after the exploit was patched.
Jan 2, 2024 evaluation finds legal hallucination rates of 69-88% on verifiable queries, a material problem in a consequential use.
Reports the specific exploit was patched, but also that the underlying vulnerabilities were not fixed. This limits the claim without contradicting it.

reviews.rationale: Research from inside the period shows PII extraction and that the vulnerability persisted after the patch (e2, with e1 and e4 as context). It also shows hallucination rates of 69-88% on legal queries (e3). Nothing in the packet shows either problem was comprehensively solved. The evidence does not cover confidential user conversations, but the contract's reading does not require it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: An unhedged 'will remain an issue' about OpenAI's candor, with no deadline. That makes it a scorable forecast.

contract.note: Reading the claim as continued, substantiated public disputes over OpenAI's disclosures or honesty is ordinary. It matches the transparency examples he gave, and it does not require proof of deliberate deception.

evidence.note: May 2024 Vox report, based on documents, contrasts leaders' statements with signed exit and equity documents. It includes OpenAI's apology. This is a material candor dispute.
OpenAI's response and policy changes soften the stronger accusations but confirm the dispute was real and attributable.

reviews.rationale: The early-resolution rule is met. In May 2024 a candor controversy arose after publication, backed by documents and an attributable company response (e1, e2). OpenAI's later fixes do not erase the dispute. The evidence predates the evaluation date.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Is sure to receive' is a firm forecast. The revision rightly dropped FTC as the scrutinizer, since he did not name one.

contract.note: Requiring substantive examination by an official regulator after publication is a fair, slightly demanding reading of 'considerable scrutiny'. The contract rightly does not require enforcement.

evidence.note: CMA full decision (March 2025, published April 2025). It describes a complex investigation using internal documents and information requests, and covers developments after the forecast.
CMA case chronology: invitation to comment in Dec 2023, formal launch and non-qualification decision in March 2025. The outcome limits conclusions about enforcement, not about scrutiny.

reviews.rationale: A dated official record after publication (e1) establishes a detailed regulatory examination of the Microsoft-OpenAI partnership, covering its governance, compute supply and IP rights. That meets the early-resolution rule. Finding that the partnership did not qualify as a merger (e2) does not contradict a forecast of scrutiny.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: A present-tense observation that many companies were trying the software without putting it into production. In context the software is ChatGPT/OpenAI's.

contract.note: Reading 'the software' as ChatGPT follows the surrounding text. 'Many' meaning a substantial group, not a majority, is ordinary. Treating surveys of all generative AI as context only is strict but defensible.

evidence.note: IBM-commissioned survey with Nov 2023 fieldwork: 42% of enterprises exploring generative AI. It does not isolate ChatGPT, and exploring does not exclude production use.
O'Reilly survey fieldwork was in September, outside the period. It covers generative AI in general, with 18% of respondents reporting production use.

reviews.rationale: Both surveys point to widespread generative-AI experimentation, but neither measures ChatGPT specifically. Neither cleanly separates trial use from production use, and O'Reilly's fieldwork falls outside the period. Under the contract they are context only, so the packet does not settle the claim.
